newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia counts votes by candlelight in close poll.
newsitem.headline: Liberia counts votes by candlelight in close poll.

text.p: A candlelit count of ballot papers pointed to to an unexpectedly close race in elections intended to rescue Liberia from its devastating civil war.

Spot assessments by reporters of the count at polling stations after voting on Saturday showed former warlord Charles Taylor and ex-United Nations official Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, two of 12 presidential candidates, both polling well.

Electoral authorities have banned publication of unofficial results, promising to start issuing partial returns from Sunday night or Monday morning. It will not be until Wednesday at the earliest when Liberians' verdict becomes clear.

Taylor, 49, is blamed for starting the country's civil war in 1989, but his forceful character is seen by many as the kind of leadership needed in the immediate post-war period. He has vastly superior resources to his election rivals and ran a well-oiled electioneering machine.
"God willing, we expect to be elected by a landslide, giving us the mandate that we need coming out of a war situation," a confident Taylor said after casting his vote.
Asked about the possibility of losing, he added:
"We are all winners at this point. I don't think these elections are about losers. These elections are about building this nation to go into the new millenium."

Johnson-Sirleaf entered the political fray late but quickly built up a groundswell of support based on an image of integrity and good contacts with aid donors. Liberian analysts say she could benefit from a ganging-up of Taylor's enemies if it came to a runoff poll between the two.
"Taylor will lose if he goes into a runoff with Johnson- Sirleaf," said one.
Johnson-Sirleaf, 58, said she believed Liberians had voted wisely. "I feel great. I think the Liberian people are ready for change...ready for a woman (president)."
Despite fears of violence because of bitter rivalries among armed factions, voting passed off peacefully under the scrutiny of more than 500 foreign monitors and regional peacekeeping troops.
Elections commission chairman Henry Andrews said reports from all the country's 13 counties showed massive turnout and orderly voting.
"The mood was good and we have not had any reports about violence or any trouble," he told an interviewer for Voice of America radio.
The West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG, which has policed Liberia since 1990, provided security, stationing soldiers at each polling station. It also transported ballot boxes.
"Everything went smoothly. No trouble was reported," force commander General Victor Malu told Reuters.

As a first step towards elections, ECOMOG has disarmed Liberian guerrillas responsible for the war that killed more than 150,000 people. More than half the pre-war population of 2.5 million is displaced and the economy shattered.
The elections come soon before the 150th birthday on July 26 of the country, founded by freed American slaves as Africa's first modern republic.
Voters were also electing 26 senators and 64 lower house deputies in the poll, based on proportional representation.
